articles.title: Democrats are at Cop31 to show that the US has not abandoned the fight against climate change
articles.author: Natasha Lindstaedt, Professor in the Department of Government, University of Essex
paras: The results of the US midterms on November 3 delivered a resounding victory for the Democrats, and a major loss for US president Donald Trump and the Republican party.

Gaining control of the Senate and the House of Representatives has emboldened the Democrats, giving them a renewed sense of political legitimacy and a mandate to pursue their agenda. But will this shift translate into meaningful changes in US climate change policy?

The Democratic sweep will change the political dynamics around US climate policy and how the country cooperates with the international community on this issue. Although there was no official US presence at the 2025 Cop conference, held in Brazil, a coalition of 100 local US leaders, including governors, mayors and other top city and state officials, attended as part of the US Climate Alliance. Former US vice-president Al Gore, and former US secretary of state John Kerry are part of an unofficial US group at the 2026 gathering.
Kerry said in a speech there: “Americans are committed to taking back their future, and we will build and rebuild our partnerships as we do that.”

Being on the ground at Cop is important. As the US has a decisive role to play in global climate policy, sending a non-official coalition signals that many Americans are still working to combat climate change.

Trump has repeatedly stated that climate change is a hoax and refused to attend the Cop31 climate talks being held in Turkey. But 20 Democratic members of Congress will be attending, although they have been denied official state department funding for the trip.

During the first and second Trump administrations, the US has been an outlier among wealthy countries when it comes to fighting climate change. Trump has actively backed the use of fossil fuels, undermining clean energy projects, and rolled back legislation that stipulated emission standards for vehicles.

Trump also weakened greenhouse gas reporting requirements and methane regulation. Then in February 2026, the Trump administration rescinded the Environmental Protection Agency’s 2009 finding that greenhouse gases threaten the health and welfare of the public, which had regulated the emissions from new cars and other vehicles. This had provided the legal foundation for regulation under the Clean Air Act.

On the international front, Trump was equally determined to undermine global efforts to fight climate change. Famously, he withdrew from the Paris agreement, part of a global initiative to address climate change, and refused to attend Cop summits. But the Democrats’ seismic midterm win may be a sign of optimism for those fighting to address climate change.
Data centres are big issue

The biggest issues of the midterms were affordability, corruption and the Iran war, but issues related to fighting climate change were also on voters’ list. There is growing concern about data centres. As many as 56% of US voters felt that data centres and AI were either a major or even crucial factor in influencing who they voted for, with only 13% saying it was not a factor at all.

Data centres require millions of gallons of water for cooling systems, and this is expected to rise to 73 billion litres of water a year by 2028. Over half of planned AI facilities in the US will be situated in areas that have significant water shortages or drought conditions.

After the midterms, Zoe Lofgren, a Democrat, is likely to become the chair of the House of Representatives’ committee on science, space and technology once the new session starts in January. She wants to tackle the administration’s “climate denialism”.
Lofgren’s leadership, along with new Democratic members of the committee, may offer it more power to reverse some of the Trump administration’s changes to science policy.

However, the Democrat midterm wins will not mean that the US is automatically back at the negotiating table at Cop nor that the US will be able to rejoin the Paris Accords while Trump is president. Trump still has the power to make these decisions and can continue to keep the US out of international climate initiatives, regardless of who controls Congress. The US Constitution says nothing about withdrawing from treaties, which creates uncertainty for what the Senate’s role might be.

The election, however, does signal that there is considerable domestic opposition to his approach. And while Congress has not passed follow-up legislation prohibiting presidential withdrawal from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), it has continued to fund several UNFCCC initiatives. During the Biden administration, the US significantly increased climate finance from US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion) a year in 2021 to US$9.5 billion in 2023.

Democrats could also push back on Trump’s current policies, using their power to hold hearings, investigate the administration’s dismantling of climate programmes and challenge cuts to scientific research. The Democrats can also use the power of Congress’s control of spending to protect or restore funding to some of these environmental initiatives.

They could also try to introduce legislation that reinstates some of the clean energy initiatives that had been implemented in past administrations to strengthen emissions standards and support clean energy. The big issue, however, is that Trump has made it clear that he is going to be very active in using his veto power, and without a two-thirds majority in Congress, the Democrats will not be able to override this.
What does this mean globally?

What this all means is that the world cannot expect the US to be a reliable and constructive partner at Cop with Trump still in power. Trump will probably continue to forge ahead with expanding fossil fuel production, while weakening international climate cooperation, even if the electorate disapproves of these policies.

Ironically, Trump’s greatest contribution to the fight against climate change was his initiation of the war with Iran, which helped to cut global fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions by 0.4% due the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But climate scientists note this is not a long-term solution.

While the Democrats’ electoral victory offers a glimmer of hope for renewed climate action, both domestically and internationally, restoring US climate leadership will take time, especially while Trump remains in power.

articles.title: Transforming climate policy into creative writing: an alternative way to experience UN summits
articles.author: Bernadette McBride, Lecturer in Creative Writing, Liverpool Hope University
paras: Formal agendas of climate summits can provide a rich source of material for creative writers. The craft of imaginative storytelling can help cut through jargon and render the ecological stakes more immediate, relatable and urgently felt.

Every year, I facilitate an intensive university course on reimagining climate futures through eco-focused creative writing. In 2024, that short course coincided with the UN climate summit, Cop29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. That was a controversial choice for climate talks, as the host nation stated it intended to expand its gas production by up to a third over the subsequent decade.
The goals of my creative writing workshop were to write with climate realism in mind, deliberately steering clear of worn, apocalyptic, end-of-the-world tropes.

The group was varied, ranging from younger undergraduates interested in climate activism to seasoned eco-poets and students from unrelated disciplines such as natural sciences. To ground our discussions in live events, I used several breaking news reports concerning Cop29 alongside extracts from official agendas documents and programme overviews as prompts for creative writing.

I was genuinely struck by how riled the students became when responding to the commitments outlined in Cop29 and broader international environmental policy. The participants were deeply critical of these promises. The interesting thing was how this fuelled and filled the room with lively, topical discussions, driving them to produce creative work that pushed boundaries.

The second part of the course coincided with a severe weather warning labelled a “danger to life” by the Met Office. We sat and watched streetlights swaying dangerously outside the classroom window in Liverpool as Storm Bert battered the country in late November 2024.

Just a week earlier, I had shared a UK government emergency preparedness brief as another writing stimulus. We had read the short story Outage by fiction writer Ian Critchley, about an older couple facing disability and struggling to cope in a power cut. I asked students to imagine a character forced to navigate that exact official guidance amid an unfolding crisis.

As a point of reference, we examined Megan Hunter’s novel-turned-film The End We Start From, starring Jodie Comer. The narrative follows a heavily pregnant protagonist, in labour and frantically calling emergency services as her London home fills with water – but, because of the widespread flooding, she finds there is no assistance. Those scenes highlight the worrying limitations of standard advice to simply “call for help” during the world catastrophes that Cop summits seek to address.
When the hypothetical scenarios we had all imagined and creatively written about became part of reality as Storm Bert hit, it felt like an eerie wake-up call.

Policy jargon, though often dense and alienating, can serve as an effective springboard for discussing difficult realities. It can give writers an accessible entry point, and a climate summit can provide a tangible event to focus on. The official Cop29 agenda, along with local council contingency policies, directly inspired more than ten distinctive poems and short stories.

The emotions evoked by these policy frameworks are more than enough to encourage creative writing that capture both the fragile hopes and real fears bound up with our climate present and future. While decision-makers may not always prove reliable narrators of our shared future, the institutional platforms they command do provide raw material for those of us who want to tell the true human and more-than-human stories.

Global summits can provoke a radical reimagining of ecological futures. As Cop31 takes place this month in Antalya, Turkey, the world public must examine these official pledges, especially those that falter or remain unfulfilled. These contested spaces represent the very realities writers must capture and hold at the front of their minds.

As the author Amitav Ghosh has questioned in his 2016 book The Great Derangement: Climate Change and the Unthinkable, where is the serious fiction about climate change? Writing through a postcolonial lens, Ghosh highlights that contemporary literature still suffers from a shortage of narratives addressing environmental crises beyond the dominant western perspective.

Because UN climate summits bring together delegations from across the globe, they offer vital opportunities to register and articulate multiple perspectives from frontline populations, from low-lying small island developing states to large industrial nations.

articles.title: COP31: Governments are failing to rein in emissions from their own power plants
articles.author: Don Grant, Professor of Sociology, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: World leaders meeting at the annual U.N. climate summit in November 2026 are wrestling with a persistent challenge: how to get countries to follow through on their commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions that are warming the planet.

One of the biggest problems has long been fossil fuel power plants, but new research shows that one type of power plant in particular has been slowest to change: those owned by the very governments making the promises and writing the laws.

My colleagues and I examined carbon dioxide emissions from thousands of fossil-fueled power plants across 134 countries. What we found reveals an important hurdle to achieving the world’s goals for keeping climate change in check.

Although countries have adopted a variety of pricing, regulatory and subsidy measures designed to curb the emissions of the electricity sector, the effectiveness of these climate policies depends on utilities responding to them.

We found that power plants owned by governments had the highest emissions as a group and didn’t cut their emissions as quickly as investor-owned facilities did in response to most policies. That does not necessarily mean they are violating policy requirements, but they were slower to move.
This matters because governments control nearly two-thirds of the world’s electricity-generating capacity.

The results suggest that to limit global warming, governments need to do more than just enact climate policies – they need to ensure that all plants translate those policies into meaningful emissions cuts.
Who owns the plants matters for climate policy
Of the 13,661 power plants that my colleagues Minh Anh Ly and Musabber Ali Chisty and I studied, 5,149 were government-owned – about 38% of them.

But those government-owned plants were responsible for 69% of the carbon emissions, based on the plants we reviewed. Together, power plants are the largest source of climate-warming carbon pollution globally.

On average, we found that government-owned power plants emitted roughly 910,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide annually – three times the average of 290,000 tons for investor-owned plants and over eight times the average of 109,000 for cooperatively owned plants.
Part of the reason for the difference is that governments often invest in large power plants that burn the dirtiest fuel – coal.

However, we also compared the plants’ emissions in 2018 to their emissions a decade earlier and looked at different national policies that were applied over that time. We found some interesting results.
Several policies were statistically associated with investor-owned power plants cutting their emissions from 2009 to 2018, including:
Pricing policies such as carbon taxes that charge companies for emissions released and emission trading systems that set limits that tighten over time.
Fossil fuel subsidy reforms that cut federal support for using fossil fuels.
Regulation policies like air pollution standards and banning and phasing out coal plants.
Renewable portfolio standards that require utilities to expand their use of renewable energy.
Subsidy policies that increase renewable energy use.
But when it came to government-owned power plants, only renewable portfolio standards were associated with significant emissions cuts. The other policies had little effect on their emissions.
These differences also appeared when we examined the stringency of policies, meaning how demanding the policy is, and the amount of time utilities have had to adjust to the policies.
Why governments struggle to clean up
So, what might explain why government-owned utilities respond differently?

Government ownership creates competing pressures that other plants are less subject to. For example, state-owned utilities may be expected to provide affordable electricity, support job growth and generate tax revenue for governments. In countries dependent on payments from companies that extract fossil fuels, utilities may also face political pressure to keep coal and gas facilities operating.

South Africa’s state-owned utility, Eskom, is a prime example. It runs a fleet of aging coal-fired power plants that make it the country’s biggest polluter. But it also provides about 90% of South Africa’s power, and when the country has faced power shortages, it has at times violated emissions standards. Despite years of climate talks, Eskom’s emissions fell little in the 2010s. They have fallen about 16% since 2019, in part due to power outages and more people relying on home solar.

The extra pressure may make it harder for government-owned power plants to reduce their emissions than for private utilities that are accountable to fewer stakeholders and can respond more directly to financial incentives to shift toward cleaner production.

There is also a potential conflict when the same government both regulates and owns a utility. Officials may be reluctant to impose costs that could raise electricity prices or require public subsidies. Our study did not measure enforcement, so we couldn’t establish that publicly owned facilities receive special treatment or disregard legal requirements.
What world leaders can do differently

Our findings suggest that in addition to persuading governments to adopt and enforce more ambitious climate policies, negotiators at the U.N. climate talks will need to get governments to ensure that the power plants they own actually respond to those policies.
Here are three ways governments could do more to get their own power plants to cut emissions.

Governments could follow the example of Ireland and establish emissions-reductions targets specifically for publicly owned utilities and tie managers’ performance reviews, investment approvals and public reporting to measurable progress. Targets are more likely to get attention when managers are held accountable for meeting them. Ireland’s emissions from electricity production fell by more than a quarter from 2019, when it added emissions-reduction targets, to 2025.

They could also do more to address the financial and political constraints their utilities face. In Morocco, for example, international financing helped a state-owned agency expand solar power while limiting costs to electricity consumers. Similar measures, combined with assistance for communities affected by coal-plant closures, could make emissions reductions more feasible.

And governments could pay closer attention to emissions of individual plants as opposed to power sectors as a whole. Publishing comparable annual plant-level emissions and flagging facilities with persistently high pollution would reveal whether sector-wide gains are masking a lack of progress at specific plants.

None of this is to suggest that privatization is the answer to climate change. Government-owned power plants offer special advantages, like coordinating long-term investment and providing reliable electricity in underserved areas. The data shows, however, that for governments to meet their obligations, they need to look closely at their own plants’ emissions, as well.

articles.title: Turkey hosts UN climate summit while pursuing new fossil fuel projects
articles.author: Ezgi Unsal, Lecturer in Development Economics, SOAS, University of London
paras: Turkey is making electrification a central theme of this year’s UN climate summit, Cop31, which it is currently hosting in the Mediterranean city of Antalya alongside Australia. The ambition is to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from 20% today to 35% by 2035.

But there is a tension in this agenda. More electrification will only cut emissions if the electricity comes from cleaner sources. In Turkey, coal and natural gas still account for more than half of electricity generation, while the country is also pursuing new oil and gas exploration deals. Ahead of a speech at the summit, the country’s president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan announced what he called the “encouraging” discovery of two new oilfields.

Turkey occupies an unusual position under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the overall treaty under which the annual climate summits and the Paris agreement emissions targets operate. When the convention was established in 1992, it divided countries into three main groups according to their economic circumstances and responsibilities for tackling climate change.

Annex I countries include industrialised nations and economies in transition that are expected to take the lead in cutting emissions. Annex II is a smaller group of wealthy industrialised nations also required to provide financial and technological support to developing countries. Most developing countries fall outside these annexes and are classified as Non-Annex I.

Turkey was originally placed in both Annex I and II as a member of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) group of largely high-income countries. However, it argued that its economic circumstances and historically low levels of emissions warranted differentiated treatment from other OECD members.

In 2001, it secured a unique compromise, and became the only country in the world to be removed from Annex II while staying in Annex I, with other countries formally recognising its “special circumstances”.

This left Turkey in a diplomatic limbo. It was no longer obliged to provide climate finance for developing countries, but its Annex I status meant it could not access some of the international funding available to them. The dispute over its eligibility for this support continued for years and was one factor that delayed Turkey’s ratification of the Paris agreement until 2021.

Since then, Turkey has secured substantial international support for its energy transition. Most notably, it secured a US$3.2 billion (£2.4 billion) financing package from the World Bank, France, Germany and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development. This is funding renewable energy and energy efficiency, alongside efforts to secure private investment.

However, access to finance is only part of the problem. A round table of UN-affiliated staff and academic experts held in July 2026 found that Turkey’s national climate commitments tend to articulate ambition without specifying how exactly this will be achieved. Successful pilots rarely turn into actual policy. Likewise, the report from the round table calls for Cop31 to be an “implementation Cop” that prioritised delivering on existing commitments over announcing new ones.

Despite rapid growth in renewable energy capacity, Turkey remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels to generate electricity. Coal accounted for 33% of the country’s electricity generation in 2025, while natural gas supplied another 22%. This means phasing out coal will require a sustained strategic effort.

Turkey adopted its first climate law in 2025, which codified an ambitious target for net-zero emissions by 2053. In this context, prioritising the rhetoric of electrification at Cop31 over phasing out coal might reveal a serious limitation of Turkey’s commitment to its climate goals.

This contradiction is also apparent in Turkey’s recent deals to expand its exploration for natural gas and oil, despite its net-zero target. In early 2026, state-owned Turkish Petroleum signed agreements with fossil fuel multinationals ExxonMobil, Chevron and BP to explore and develop further oil and gasfields.

Activists have also criticised the appointment of major conglomerates linked to environmental disputes as official summit sponsors. Cop31’s “sustainable transformation partner” is a firm that plans to build more coal power plants, while another sponsor is linked to widespread deforestation to make way for coal mines.

There are also worries about how inclusive the summit will prove to be. Speakers in the host-managed Green Zone have been required to sign a declaration pledging compliance with Turkish law and “public morality”, omitting standard UN protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. The declaration also warned delegates against “interfering in internal affairs”, which could result in the silencing of political dissent.

Turkey’s unusual position in the international climate system explains some of the difficulties it has faced in its transition. But it cannot explain away the country’s continuing dependence on coal and gas, its pursuit of new fossil fuel projects or the questions surrounding the inclusiveness of the summit itself. With Australia leading the negotiations and Turkey hosting the event, Cop31 highlights these contradictions.

articles.title: States like Samoa face brutal 2027 storm season – every dollar of ‘climate cash’ counts for small islands
articles.author: Emily Wilkinson, Principal Research Fellow, Global Risks and Resilience, ODI Global
paras: Every nation is grappling with climate change, but a super El Niño is about to collide with the 2026-27 South Pacific cyclone season. This presents one of the toughest challenges yet for the world’s small island nations.

Samoa is on high alert. These islands have had a turbulent recent history with drought, heat and cyclones. In the 1980s, the El Niño cycle (when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual) caused severe drought and acute water shortages, plus a heightened risk of tropical cyclones. In Samoa, families still recall the unbearable heat that withered once-lush green forests into tinder-dry matchsticks, sparking fires across the villages of Asau and Aopo.

As Samoans contend with the complex effects of El Niño in the coming months, they’ll also be experiencing the everyday consequences of climate change: 70% of the population and infrastructure are located in low-lying coastal areas. Sea levels have risen by as much as 31cm over the last three decades. This puts islanders at greater risk from flooding, more frequent and severe cyclones and saltwater intrusion (whereby dense, saline seawater infiltrates freshwater) damaging their crops.

In talanoa (story‑based dialogue, common in the Pacific) with family in Vaisala, Utusamia Barbara Carter told one of us (George Carter) how “today, the challenge is different but no less alarming. The sea is slowly rising, and our homeland is gradually being swallowed by the ocean”.

Perversely, in the short term, El Niño can lead to both high and low sea levels. During the cycle extremely low sea levels (referred to in Samoa as taimasa) can expose shallow reefs, which cause coral to die off, while the long-term trend of sea-level rise is caused by climate change.
Samoan traditions and identity are deeply tied to the land, ocean, sky and people (kinship). They and other Pacific Islanders want to stay put and maintain their way of life.

Samoa is one of 39 island nations known as small island developing states, a group that is recognised by the UN as being exceptionally vulnerable to climate change. What is new is the scale and intensity of the risk, given the compounding effects of climate change, which are occurring at a time when international cooperation on climate action is fraying.

Small island developing states continue to struggle to access adequate levels of funding to boost their climate resilience and adapt their infrastructure. The implementation of this climate finance involves long delays and red tape. Many of them feel that the world’s powers are increasingly treating them as a marginal concern, compared to more pressing issues of economic prosperity, peace and global security.
This is a big mistake. The resilience of small island developing states is increasingly bound up with all three of these issues.

These nations are spread out across the Caribbean, Pacific, Atlantic and Indian Ocean and South China Sea. They make up less than 0.5% of the world’s total land mass and less than 1% of the global population. Individually, they have little economic or military power.
These island nations may be small in landmass and population, but they govern vast ocean territories; and many sit at the centre of intensifying geopolitical competition.

Small island developing states represent 38 out of a total of 193 UN member states so they account for around 20% of votes at the UN. They have repeatedly exercised influence far beyond their economic weight. The 1.5°C temperature goal at the heart of the UN’s Paris climate agreement might never have been secured without sustained pressure from the Alliance of Small Island States, the negotiating bloc representing these island nations.

Similarly, the landmark judgment on climate change and state responsibility by the International Court for Justice in July 2025 was spearheaded by the Pacific island nation of Vanuatu. Small island developing states are, by and large, among the most successful post-colonial democracies, and their regions remain largely peaceful.

The vast ocean spaces that small island nations oversee are known as exclusive economic zones. Within these zones, countries govern everything from fishing to deep-sea mining. The exclusive economic zones that small island developing states govern span 30% of the world’s oceans. On average, that is 28 times their combined landmass. These waters encompass precious marine ecosystems like seagrasses and coral reefs that regulate the climate, support fisheries and absorb carbon.

Even with their vulnerability to extreme weather many small island developing states have built successful economies with high levels of per capita income since independence. Entrepreneurs in small island developing states are producing green technologies and digital services with applications beyond their domestic economies.
Australia plans to use its presidency of the UN climate summit Cop31 to highlight the special circumstances of small island developing states, but it must also achieve some tangible results.

One big step forward would be to improve access to existing flows of already pledged climate cash that isn’t reaching the right places fast enough. Island states need low-interest loans and grants, known as concessional finance, so they can invest in their own resilience without getting deeper into debt.

The new Pacific Resilience Facility is a climate finance mechanism owned and led by Pacific people that launched earlier this year. It is a good example of how wealthier countries might help islands like Samoa prepare for the new reality.

Wealthy nations could also recognise specific small island vulnerabilities by ensuring there is a “climate exception”. Small island nations whose income levels mean they are no longer eligible for official development assistance, could be made eligible again but just for assistance that is for building climate resilience. This would mean that highly vulnerable small islands with higher incomes don’t get shut out of aid budgets that will be essential to their survival in years to come.

articles.title: Andy Burnham and climate change: where does the prime minister really stand?
articles.author: James Jackson, Lecturer and Research Fellow, School of Social Sciences, University of Manchester
paras: Since becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham has set out a relatively ambitious political agenda. He has outlined plans for a national care service, a “Great British Grid” and suggested a rethink of the UK’s relationship with the European Union.
But one big omission of Burnham’s agenda is climate policy. Amid the proposals that put clear water between him and his predecessor Keir Starmer, Burnham’s climate agenda remains unknown.

The prime minister has reiterated his intention to reach net zero by 2050 (though this target is contentious due to whether it actually reflects climate science as well as the extent to which it depends upon as yet unavailable technology). He has also pledged to attend Cop31, the UN climate summit currently underway in Turkey, in person. However, the budget – Burnham’s first real opportunity to set out his vision – raised concerns about whether his political rhetoric could translate into a coherent climate policy.

The budget revealed that increased defence spending would come at the cost of £3 billion of cuts at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Subsidies for heat pumps, boilers, the warm homes plan, hydrogen and carbon capture and storage were the most prominent policies to be culled. This not only limits the UK’s green industrial policy, but suggests that energy security is still not considered to be part of national security.
Energy security and rising bills

For years, the UK has been misaligned with its own carbon budgets set under the Climate Change Act 2008. After the Conservatives began to question the objective of net zero towards the end of their term in office, the election of the first Labour government in 14 years was expected to mark a turning point.

Burnham’s climate position has become entwined (and somewhat undermined) by energy security concerns following the so-called fossilflationary pressures caused by the the US and Israel’s conflict with Iran. This has fed into the licensing of the Jackdaw gasfield 150 miles east of Aberdeen. This is part of Burnham’s self-described “pragmatic” approach to new drilling in the North Sea.

The initial justification was that the move would improve energy security by increasing the domestic supply of oil and gas. But critics say that increasing supply has little to no effect on domestic bills, as prices are set by international markets. Revenues made from the project will be used to finance an Energy Wealth Fund to invest in green technologies elsewhere.

Then there’s the cost of living. As winter approaches, an increasing number of households will have to choose between heating and eating. In response, Chancellor John Healey’s budget removed green levies from consumer bills. These levies fund environmental programmes such as renewable schemes, but the money will now be sourced from general taxation.
This does reduce bills in the short term. But the shift, combined with other cuts, raises doubts over the long term.

It’s argued that removing green levies from bills will reduce the relative cost of energy. This is a salient argument as the UK approaches a period of higher energy demand to heat the country’s homes. But critics say that reducing support for green energy infrastructure will delay the advent of abundant cheap energy.
Political and economic tests

Labour now has two challenges. The first is the political bind the party finds itself in. Its manifesto does not contain anything resembling an ambitious climate policy. Although Burnham represents a change at the top, he has not won the right to depart from the platform upon which Starmer was elected.
Whether this represents a constraint on Burnham’s political vision or just more of the same on a limited climate policy is up for debate.

The second is an economic bind due to the UK’s tight fiscal position. This is despite taxation being at a historically high level – much of which has come from “fiscal drag” as taxpayers are pulled into higher tax bands.

The broader issues are that ten-year UK gilt yields – the rate the government pays on its debt – have risen to 5.13%. The irony of the rise in gilt yields is that they have increased primarily because of “fossilflation” as supply-side shocks have fed into energy prices.
As a result, the Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years, to 4%. This will further increase borrowing costs and make life less affordable for UK households.

And yet Labour’s propositions only put its climate policy into further doubt. It remains to be seen whether it will grant a licence for the Rosebank oil field, west of Shetland, which is larger than Jackdaw. Unless the government bends to political pressure, Burnham and energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh could make the same arguments about energy security again.

In the meantime, Burnham has signalled his desire to raise tariffs on Chinese green technology to align the UK more closely to the EU. This would be a bid to answer security worries, but tariffs on the cheapest and largest source of green technology places climate second to geopolitical concerns.
Under Burnham, climate policy has, at best, been lost amid the prime minister’s broader political platform. At worst, he has concluded it is a price worth paying to achieve his other objectives.

articles.title: 5 ways countries stymie climate negotiations without actually saying ‘no’
articles.author: Shannon Gibson, Professor (Teaching) of Environmental Studies, Political Science and International Relations, USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences
paras: Nearly every country in the world has acknowledged that climate change is a serious problem. It’s hard to ignore, as billions of people suffer through increasingly destructive storms and extreme heat.

In response, most governments have promised repeatedly to cut greenhouse gas emissions that are driving global temperatures higher. Yet those emissions are still hitting record levels, and global negotiations over how to slow climate change routinely end with weak promises.

There’s a reason: All it takes to water down a deal during these negotiations – the 2026 U.N. climate conference started Nov. 9 – are a few voices obstructing progress, often without ever saying “no,” and all the while maintaining the appearance of being a climate leader.

As a professor of environmental studies and international relations at the University of Southern California, I’ve attended and observed international climate negotiations for over a decade. My research lab investigates climate justice concerns and the forces that obstruct progress at the global U.N. climate talks.

As world leaders and their negotiators meet for the latest climate talks, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 9-20, you can also pick out who is obstructing progress. Here are five tactics among many that powerful people at these conferences use to delay, weaken or redirect meaningful action while still appearing committed to addressing climate change:
“We don’t have the money” is a familiar refrain at U.N. climate negotiations.

At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024, wealthy countries pointed to tight budgets, pandemic debt and rising inflation as reasons they could not meet the US$1.3 trillion in assistance that developing countries were demanding. They instead offered $300 billion annually by 2035 as a finance target.

Poorer countries that did little to cause climate change want longtime fossil fuel users to pay for the damage emissions have caused. The COP29 agreement itself estimated that developing countries’ climate needed $5.1 trillion to $6.8 trillion in total through 2030.
In reality, affordability is really about priorities.

For example, the International Institute for Sustainable Development found that governments around the world provided more than $1.2 trillion in public financial support for fossil fuels in 2024, about five times the $254 billion they provided for clean energy.

Military budgets tell a similar story. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the U.S. contributed $2 billion to the Green Climate Fund, meant to support poorer countries as they adapt to climate change, while Congress simultaneously approved at least $79 billion to help foreign countries by U.S. military weapons. Recent research points out that rising military spending makes climate goals even harder to reach because so much military activity runs on fossil fuels.
The money exists. The question is where governments choose to spend it.
2. Promise to fix it later
Another tactic is claiming that technological innovations will clean things up eventually, so drastic emissions cuts can wait or even be avoided.

This technological optimism has deep roots. In 2004, Princeton scholars Steve Pacala and Robert Socolow proposed the “stabilization wedge” approach to addressing climate change. It slices future emissions growth into 15 strategy wedges, each representing a way to cut 1 billion tons of carbon dioxide. Selecting from that menu, government could piece together a suitable emissions reduction strategy.
Renewable energy solutions such as solar and wind were proposed as wedges, but so were carbon capture and storage technologies – which would allow the burning of fossil fuels to continue.

Scientists, including one of the original authors, have claimed that the wedges approach makes a difficult problem look deceptively simple to solve. Recent reporting by ProPublica tracked money behind the wedges project back to the fossil fuel giant BP.
Yet the same logic is now present in agreements emerging from recent climate talks.
Another tactic is to agree to something, then water it down over time until it is no longer binding.

At COP26 in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2022, early drafts of the agreement called for the “phasing out” of fossil fuels. It would have been a true milestone, as it was the first time the words “fossil fuels” had appeared in a climate agreement.

However, after a late push led by India, backed by China, South Africa and others, the final text was changed to “phasedown” of “unabated” coal power instead. Additionally, the pact said nothing of oil and gas, the fuels that wealthier countries depend on most.

The first fossil fuel language in a U.N. climate pact came out diluted. Four years later, at COP30, 88 countries backed a roadmap to move the world away from using fossil fuels, but the final decision left it out.
4. Make promises, then fail to deliver
Countries are really good at making pledges to help, but not so much at providing the funding.

In 2009, wealthy countries promised developing countries $100 billion annually to help them address climate risks. They missed that target for over a decade. Even when they did claim to hit the target, they relied largely on dubious accounting, with donors counting fossil fuel projects, airports and even ice cream shops as climate aid.

The Loss and Damage Fund created at COP27 in 2021 to help countries manage disaster damage shows a similar pattern. Only about half of the roughly $822 million pledged had been paid in five years later, and the fund has not paid out a single dollar to a country hit by a disaster.

Nepal has emerged as a critical test of the fund’s integrity. After a glacier collapse triggered a sudden flood that killed more than 1,400 people in Nepal in August 2026, the government estimated the country had suffered $2.7 billion in damage. Nepal requested $20 million, and, in a first, the fund’s board agreed in October to “provisionally set aside” $21.6 million, but that’s only the beginning of the paperwork.
5. Make decisions without everyone at the table
Decisions at the U.N. climate conference are taken by consensus, meaning they’re considered adopted when no country formally objects. This act is marked by the banging of a gavel.

At COP28 in Dubai, the conference president “gaveled through” a key decision before representatives of the Alliance of Small Island States had reached the room, meaning they had no chance to object. The lead negotiator for the islands’ group told the meeting that they would have objected, as they considered it too weak to keep warming to the agreed limit of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) within reach.
In 2025, at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, a similar scene played out.

After swiftly gaveling through many decisions, the conference president failed to recognize Colombia’s request to speak until after the gavel had fallen. Colombia objected that the text of the formal decision failed to discuss a transition away from fossil fuels. The COP president later apologized but said the decision could not be reopened.
What to watch for at COP31
At COP31, my team and I will be watching for decisions about financial support, whether talk of technology crowds out reducing fossil fuel use, and who gets a voice.

Much of what matters at these conferences happens out of the spotlight. Plenary sessions, where decisions are formally adopted, are the part most people see. But the wording of those decisions is usually worked out in smaller rooms and closed-door huddles among a handful of delegations. Small delegations can’t staff every room, and some rooms are closed to observers.
My team will be tracking what happens, whose proposals survive, and what quietly drops out between drafts of the agreement text. We’ll also be paying attention to who, quietly or not, says “no.”
Ridwan Intisaar Mahbub, a graduate student in public diplomacy, and Richie Sanchez, an undergraduate student in environmental studies at USC, contributed research for this article.

articles.title: How protection of public land shapes political strategies in the American West
articles.author: Erika Allen Wolters, Associate Professor of Political Science, Oregon State University
paras: Public lands are intricately woven into the fabric of America. Years of data confirms that a majority of Americans, regardless of their political beliefs, want public lands to remain in federal hands – though not everyone agrees on how exactly those lands should be managed. And while it’s not clear that public lands were a crucial factor in the 2026 midterm election results, survey data suggests that it is an important issue in deciding whom to vote for.

Federal conservation efforts began in the late 1800s, with Yellowstone becoming the first national park in 1872. Today, 640 million acres, nearly 30% of the country’s land area, are administered by the federal government for a wide range of purposes, including conservation, forestry, grazing and energy production. These lands are held in trust by the federal government for the American people.

In our studies of the politics of the American West, where the vast majority of U.S. public lands are located, we are seeing efforts to make voters aware of candidates’ views on land protection and to use grassroots political tactics to influence management decisions.
Protesting government efforts to turn turn public spaces into private property, or to allow development on public land, are key ways people show the value they place on public lands.

In 2017, at the start of Donald Trump’s first term as president, U.S. Rep. Jason Chaffetz, a Utah Republican, proposed that the federal government transfer land to individual states. The states, underfunded and understaffed to manage the land themselves, would likely have sold the land to private interests. The response created the #KeepItPublic social media campaign and mobilized conservation groups against the bill. Land Tawney, president of Backcountry Hunters and Anglers, said, “Once that bill was introduced, the hornet’s nest was kicked.” Chaffetz pulled the bill and left Congress five months later.

And in 2025, after Trump returned to the White House, U.S. Sen. Mike Lee, a Utah Republican, proposed that Congress require the U.S. Bureau of Land Management and the U.S. Forest Service to sell between 2.2 million to 3.3 million acres of public land in 11 Western states. He said the land sale would help “address local housing needs.”

But conservation groups and other Western lawmakers, including fellow Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Sheehy and Republican U.S. Rep. Ryan Zinke, also of Montana, declared the proposal a “threat to the Montana way of life” and forced Lee to withdraw the proposal.
There isn’t available evidence to suggest that voters choose members of Congress based solely on their views or action about the management of public lands.

But elected officials often swiftly distance themselves from or outright oppose efforts to modify or eliminate public land protections. That response signals they believe their land protection stances play a role in how the public views them.

For example, Trump administration efforts to reduce Bears Ears National Monument and to swap a parcel in Yosemite National Park with a private developer met with opposition from both parties in Congress.

However, that opposition is not always successful at preventing development or natural resource extraction on public lands. In March and April 2026, both houses of Congress passed a resolution supporting mining near the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in Minnesota, despite public outcry about the potential pollution of a vast wilderness.
Public lands in election politics

In 2026, two new groups emerged to call attention to threats to public lands. Protect Wyoming and PAC for Public Lands in Idaho both formed specifically to compile and publicize elected officials’ public lands voting records, especially when those votes affect people’s rights to hunt, fish and enjoy the outdoors.

These groups may be able to tap into core land protection values broadly shared by many voters across the political spectrum. That could put more direct and consistent pressure on politicians to protect public lands.
The Trump administration has moved to limit people from mobilizing in support of public lands.

For instance, Trump’s Jan. 20, 2025, executive order declaring a “national energy emergency” has led the Department of the Interior to accelerate its review of proposals for oil and gas drilling, production and refining, and mining, along with other energy-related natural resource development.

A process that used to take one to two years has been reduced to no more than a month. That provides less time for people to review documents, understand what they say and decide how they feel about the proposals. However, 15 states are now suing the Trump administration, saying that fast-tracking violates federal law and seeking court orders to restore the previous process.

And in January 2026, the White House Council on Environmental Quality revised the rules around public comments on proposed federal land management actions. Government agencies are required under the National Environmental Policy Act to give the public a chance to comment on rule changes. It is the primary way the public can raise objections, question the thoroughness of the options, or to provide other evidence to help inform policy. The council significantly shortened, or in some cases eliminated, the time period during which the public may submit comments – though that decision has also been challenged in court, saying the Administrative Procedure Act requires the original amount of public comment.
Retaining the public trust

How the government handles data center development may shed further light on the political power of public lands. Back in July 2025, Trump issued an executive order seeking to “utilize federally owned land and resources for the expeditious and orderly development of data centers.”
In fall 2026, media outlets and advocacy groups called attention to efforts to develop data centers on public lands, including at least 17 computing campuses in six states.
Nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose data centers being built in their communities. Some politicians have questioned the deals on federal land.

These centers were on the minds of voters in the midterm elections, nowhere more than in the Nevada gubernatorial race, where the Democratic challenger won on a platform to oppose projects on federal land. Voter discontent may not stop the Trump administration from moving forward, but it all but guarantees that data centers on public lands will be an issue in the 2028 general election. The degree to which the opposition gains political momentum could be another indicator of how the American public will act to continue to demand that public lands remain in public hands.

articles.title: Starling numbers are declining – we’re investigating whether their spectacular murmuration displays are changing too
articles.author: Adam Hart, Professor of Conservation Ecology, University of Gloucestershire
paras: Every autumn, from city centres to wetlands, starling murmurations attract crowds of spectators. Thousands of birds fill the sky, twisting and turning in extraordinary waves as the sun sets. An entire flock moves as one, creating shapes that shift and dissolve as quickly as they appear.

But Britain’s breeding starling population has declined dramatically over recent decades, while changes in climate, migration and habitats are reshaping the lives of many birds. Could these wider changes also be affecting murmurations? By repeating a major citizen-science survey we carried out 12 years ago, we’re hoping to find out whether these spectacular displays are changing in size, timing or location.

According to the British Trust for Ornithology, the UK’s breeding starling population declined by 61% between 1995 and 2024. This is part of a wider pattern of bird declines: the UK’s farmland bird population index has fallen by 62% since 1970, with intensification of farming playing a major role. But that doesn’t necessarily mean individual murmurations are becoming smaller. Changes in where birds gather, when they arrive and how they behave could all influence the displays we see each winter.

Climate change may also be playing a part in shifting patterns and timings of murmuration displays. Britain’s winter starling population includes large numbers of birds arriving from continental Europe. As winter conditions change, so might their migration patterns, potentially affecting the timing, location and size of murmurations. Changes in food availability and roosting habitat could also be important.

Our original citizen-science project began in 2014. Working with the Royal Society of Biology, we harnessed people power to record murmurations between 2014 and 2016. Volunteer citizen scientists submitted more than 3,000 observations, noting the size, duration and location of murmurations, plus the presence of any birds of prey. Observations from 23 countries provided an unusually large dataset.

Back then, our main question wasn’t whether murmurations were changing, but why they happened at all. Over the last 20 years, scientists have made considerable progress in understanding how thousands of birds coordinate their movements, with each responding to its neighbours to produce those extraordinary patterns. But why do starlings gather in such spectacular formations in the first place?

One explanation was that the displays helped attract birds to communal roosts, where gathering in large numbers might provide warmth. Another was that murmurations helped protect starlings from predators such as peregrine falcons and sparrowhawks. Moving together in a dense, constantly changing flock could make it harder for a predator to single out a specific bird, while providing more eyes to detect approaching danger.

Our findings, published in 2017, provided strong support for this predator avoidance explanation. Murmurations tended to be larger and last longer when predators were present, particularly when they approached or attacked the flock. Although we couldn’t establish cause and effect from these observations alone, the evidence suggested that avoiding predators was a major reason for these spectacular displays, with attracting birds to a warm communal roost on cold nights being a secondary factor.

Our research also revealed a seasonal pattern in murmuration size and duration, with day length associated with how long displays lasted. Twelve years later, we are exploring whether those patterns have persisted, and whether the relationships between murmurations, predators and temperatures remain the same.

Once again, we’re asking the public to help. By recording where and when they see murmurations, how many birds are involved, how long the displays last and whether predators are present, observers can help us investigate whether this extraordinary behaviour is changing.

A starling murmuration isn’t just a feast for the eyes. As the birds sweep low overhead, you can hear the collective rush of thousands of wings. And there’s another sensory experience, too: a shower of starling droppings. Somehow, even that adds to the occasion, although we’d recommend taking an umbrella.

If you’re lucky enough to witness a murmuration this autumn or winter, take a moment to enjoy the spectacle and log what you see. Your observations could help reveal whether one of nature’s most extraordinary displays is changing.

articles.title: Flesh-eating screwworm is spreading in the US, threatening livestock and wildlife – hunters can be the first line of defense
articles.author: Jacob Dykes, Assistant Professor of Wildlife Management, Mississippi State University
paras: For the first time in over 50 years, an infestation of the flesh-eating fly known as the New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) is spreading on the U.S. mainland, and it is putting livestock and other animals at risk.
The New World screwworm doesn’t just attack cattle. All warm-blooded animals are susceptible, including deer and elk, as well as small game, waterfowl and pets.
That means hunters headed to the field this fall may be the most important line of defense for spotting this destructive parasite and keeping it from spreading further.

As co-directors of the Mississippi State University deer lab, we believe the country’s millions of hunters can serve as a powerful early warning system by keeping a close eye on the state of wildlife they see. Wildlife agencies are already asking them to be vigilant and report any signs of screwworm infestations.
The problem with screwworm

Unlike other blowflies, New World screwworm larvae feed on living tissue rather than dead tissue. They lay eggs in open wounds or mucosal openings, such as the eyes and nose of livestock, deer or elk.

Wounds as small as tick bites or scratches, as well as natural openings such as the umbilical stump on newborns or on deer’s pedicles, where their antlers grow and are shed, can attract these parasites.
Once the eggs hatch, the maggots burrow into the animal’s flesh and feed, enlarging the wound and attracting more flies. Over time, this leads to infection and death.
How the US eradicated screwworm in the past
All warm-blooded animals are susceptible to the New World screwworm, but America has seen firsthand the harm they can cause to livestock.
In the 1950s, livestock producers in the U.S. Southwest lost up to US$100 million annually to New World screwworm infections, equivalent to over $1 billion today.

The nation was eventually able to eradicate the New World screwworm from the mainland in 1966 using a combination of treating infected animals and raising hundreds of millions of sterilized male flies and releasing them in infested areas.

The New World screwworm has a life cycle of only about 21 days, and each female mates only once. Because of that, inundating areas with sterile male flies for a few months, which equates to a few generations of flies, can eradicate a screwworm population.

Over time, sterile flies were used to push the New World screwworm further south, where they had been contained behind the Darién Gap, Panama’s narrow border region with Colombia. Sterile flies kept the parasite south of Panama for years, but the movement of cattle and wildlife likely brought it north again. Since 2022, the parasites have been reproducing and moving farther northward. There have been hundreds of detections in Mexico and now in the U.S.
The Florida Key deer infestation

Wildlife have received far less attention than livestock during screwworm infestations, with one exception: In July 2016, the New World screwworm was detected in the Florida Keys in an endangered deer population: the Florida Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium).

At the time, the Florida Key deer population was estimated at only about 800 to 1,000 individuals. Because they were endangered and isolated, primarily on the islands of Big Pine Key and No Name Key, they were monitored more closely than most wildlife.

U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service biologists established quarantine zones. They inspected more than 16,900 animals – dogs, cats, a pig and a raccoon were also found with larvae – and they released 150 million sterile flies across the area. The islands lost 9% to 20% of the total Key Deer population, but the New World screwworm was declared eradicated there on March 23, 2017, less than a year after it was discovered.

In June 2026, screwworm was back in the United States. A rancher discovered the first New World screwworm case in a calf near La Pryor, Texas. A few more cases were confirmed in livestock and domestic animals in Texas and New Mexico.

The number of cases in animals had passed 125 as of Nov. 10, 2026, including in two elk reported by hunters in Texas. The U.S. government has started ramping up production of sterile flies to try to keep the parasites from spreading.
Although there have been only a couple of cases reported in wildlife, that isn’t necessarily reassuring.

Wildlife are far more likely to carry the parasite without being detected. Once the screwworm is detected, treatment would also be much more complicated for wildlife than for livestock, because wildlife cannot be treated individually and thus are more dependent on the use of sterile flies to eradicate screwworm.
For this reason, quickly identifying areas with New World screwworm and targeting those areas by releasing sterile flies would be more important than ever.
Tapping an army of conservationists: Hunters
Fortunately, there is an army of conservationists across the country who spend much of their time afield. These conservationists are also known as hunters.

According to the latest U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service National Survey of Fishing, Hunting, and Wildlife-Associated Recreation, nearly 11.5 million hunters pursue big game and spend part of the fall and winter in the field hunting ungulate species such as deer and elk.

White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) hunters alone are expected to harvest about 6 million deer during the 2026-27 season and will observe millions more. Hunters also review tens of millions of wildlife pictures collected each year by game cameras used for scouting.

That level of surveillance can’t be matched. New Mexico’s Department of Agriculture has already called on hunters to report any suspicious larvae, particularly in Grant and Otero counties, where screwworm has been found in livestock. Hunters of all kinds, everywhere, can help.
What to watch for as a hunter
If you’re a hunter, be on the lookout for wounded animals, especially those with visible maggots, and for unusual behaviors such as restlessness, lethargy, or biting or licking wounds.

Do not move harvested animals from the field if they show signs of a New World screwworm infection. Doing so could further spread the parasite. Instead, contact the area’s state wildlife agency, the U.S. Department of Agriculture office or a local veterinarian immediately.
As hunting seasons get underway across the country, an army of conservationists will be in the field, and they have an important role to play in detecting and managing screwworm’s spread.

Hunters already contribute to conservation through license fees, excise taxes and keeping wildlife populations at healthy densities. In the face of New World screwworm, their observations may be most valuable for protecting livestock.

articles.title: The Cop31 climate summit is betting on electrification – but still needs a plan to ditch fossil fuels
articles.author: Freddie Daley, Research Associate, Centre for Global Political Economy, University of Sussex
paras: The latest UN climate summit, Cop31, will get underway in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9. One of its key objectives is to boost electrification across the global economy – replacing petrol and diesel vehicles, gas boilers and some industrial processes that burn fossil fuels with electric alternatives.

The summit’s host, Turkey, has set a target of 35% of energy demand being met by electricity by 2035, up from around 20% today. Announcing the “35-by-35” pledge, Cop31 president Murat Kurum described it as “one of the defining features” of Turkey’s presidency, highlighting the risks of continued dependence on imported fossil fuels.

Without doubt, electrification is essential to curtailing greenhouse gas emissions, and is already gathering pace. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has declared we are living in the “age of electricity”, and if stated policy pledges hold, global electrification rates will hit 31% by 2050. The Cop31’s focus on electrification hopes to build upon and accelerate this existing trend.

But electrification alone won’t deliver a clean energy transition. Two major challenges remain: the continued expansion of fossil fuel production, and growing geopolitical competition over clean technologies where the latter is increasingly shaping governments’ climate and energy policies, as they struggle to compete with dominant “electrostates” such as China.

The Australian climate minister and Cop31’s president of negotiations has described electrification and fossil fuel reduction as “different sides of the same coin”. But they are not interchangeable. Electrification can reduce some demand for fossil fuels, but it won’t stop governments approving new projects and expanding supply.

By 2030, governments are planning to produce more than double the amount of fossil fuels than would be consistent with limiting warning to 1.5°C. More concerning is that this assessment was made before the conflict and disruption in the Middle East, which has caused the US, Brazil, Guyana, Argentina, Canada and other fossil fuel producers to increase output in the name of energy security. The UK, meanwhile, has approved the Jackdaw gasfield in a purported bid to protect jobs and keep homes warm.

The 35-by-35 target is also silent on where that additional electricity will come from. After all, a country could in theory increase its rate of electrification by burning more fossil fuels (imagine a country where every car was electric, but all that electricity came from coal).
A genuine energy transition

What’s needed is the two-pronged approach of electrifying economies while simultaneously phasing out fossil fuels and reducing their supply. This will ensure capital is reallocated to renewable energy for electrification. Governments can do this nationally or through international initiatives such as the Beyond Oil and Gas Alliance, the Clean Energy Transition Partnership and the Cop-adjacent conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

Skirting the fossil fuel issue is nothing new at these summits. It took 26 years for a formal resolution or agreement to explicitly name fossil fuels, in Glasgow in 2021. And even then it only passed with calls to “phasedown” unabated coal power and phase-out “inefficient” fossil fuel subsidies.

At Cop31, fossil fuels are entirely absent from the formal agenda. Brazil has published an extensive voluntary “roadmap” to guide governments’ phase-out efforts, but this sits outside the formal negotiations and lacks timelines.
This begs the question: is a focus on electrification a way to avoid the perennially thorny issue of fossil fuels?

Even growing demand for electricity does not guarantee a clean energy transition. The data centre boom in the US and beyond, for instance, is driving the use of gas and coal to generate electricity. The International Gas Union, a lobby group for natural gas producers, is explicitly positioning gas as a way to meet growing demand from data centres and AI.

Increasing electrification looks relatively straightforward: just encourage more renewable energy production and electric vehicles. Yet, for most of the world, this would mean overcoming security and trade tensions with China, whose dominance in clean technologies, manufacturing and rare earth processing makes it a lynchpin electrostate in a world hoping to electrify everything.

China’s dominance is near total. For the component materials of solar panels, in 2024 China controlled 93% of global polysilicon processing, 97% of wafer manufacturing – making the thin slices of silicon that form the basis of solar panels – 92% of solar cell manufacturing and 86% of solar module production. It also produced more than 80% of electric vehicle batteries in 2025. According to the IEA, China is dominant across 19 of 20 energy-related strategic minerals, averaging over 70% of processing control. Achieving global electrification targets will therefore require continued access to Chinese technologies, products and raw materials.

This runs counter to almost two decades of western policy aimed at protecting domestic industries from Chinese competition and restricting China’s technological development, most notably with semi-conductors. While these efforts have largely failed to contain Chinese innovation, an overreliance on Chinese clean technologies is increasingly seen as a “serious risk” to Europe’s economic and national security. European governments have responded with tariffs and restrictions on Chinese imports and investments, while seeking to build up their own manufacturing capacity.

Governments face a difficult dilemma. Opening their economies further to Chinese technologies could mean unpicking trade protections developed over years and create new dependencies, while refusing to cooperate with China risks slowing electrification and may even drive some governments to abandon climate and energy policies altogether because they cannot compete.
While the drive towards electrification at Cop31 is to be welcomed, it cannot be a substitute for the harder political task of securing binding commitments to phase out fossil fuels, fast and fairly.

articles.title: Don’t wash your laundry at teatime – why planning energy use can reduce your bills
articles.author: Lala Rukh, PhD Candidate, Energy, University of Galway; Atlantic Technological University
paras: For decades, judging a home’s energy performance meant asking one question: how much does it use? Labels such as energy performance certificates still ask only that.

But homes are changing. Add solar panels, a battery or an electric car, and a house starts to generate, store and sell electricity. Meanwhile, what that electricity costs depends more and more on the clock. Since June 2026, Ireland’s largest suppliers have had to offer tariffs that change every half hour. In the UK, households pay about 26p for each unit they buy, but solar owners can be paid as little as a few pence for each unit they sell.
The question has shifted from how much energy is being used to when is it being consumed? Every building is now an energy system. The clearest example of what that means is a long way from Europe.

In Pakistan, an estimated 7.3 million households, nearly one in five, now have solar panels. In the year to June 2025, panels on homes, shops, farm sheds and small factories produced the equivalent of 46% of all electricity sold through the national grid. Three lessons stand out.

First, nobody paid them to do it. There was no rooftop programme and no subsidy. Squeezed by rising tariffs and power cuts, people bought cheap panels imported from China: nearly 54 gigawatts by March 2026, roughly the capacity of the entire grid.

Second, most of it was invisible. By mid-2025, an estimated 38 gigawatts of solar was installed, generating 51 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to power every home in the UK for more than six months. Yet only 6.8 gigawatts was registered where the regulator could see it. Overall electricity sold through the nation’s grid system fell 11% in three years, and planners could not see what was replacing them.

Third, when the rules caught up, the Pakistani government changed the deal mid-boom. In February 2026, the regulator cut the price paid to new solar customers for exported power by more than two-thirds. After a backlash, those who had already applied kept the old terms. But the households who could never afford panels are left paying for an electricity supply through the nation’s grid infrastructure that fewer people use.

Pakistan is an extreme case, but the direction is global. Electricity is being priced by when it is used, not just how much. In the US, California has paid new solar owners about a quarter of the retail price for exported power since 2023. Australia, which has more midday solar than it can use, now offers households three free hours of electricity at around lunchtime.
The message is the same everywhere. Solar power is worth most when you use it yourself, or when the grid needs it, usually in the early evening.
Measuring when, not just how much

If timing matters this much, we need to measure it. As part of my PhD research, I developed a time-of-use score that rates a home on when it draws power from the grid. Electricity used in the 5pm–7pm peak counts least; electricity used in the after midnight hours, when the grid is quiet, counts most. For homes with solar, a grid interaction score does the same for the power still bought after the panels and batteries have done their work.

We applied the score to newly built, A-rated (highly energy-efficient) apartments that we monitored for a full year. Almost all of them fell into the lowest time-of-use class. On paper these were among the most efficient homes in the country, yet they leaned on the grid at the worst times. Much of their load, such as hot water, washing machines and dishwashers, could easily have moved.
You don’t need a research project to run your solar-fitted home more efficiently as an energy system. Three rules cover most of it.
Use the sun first. Run the dishwasher, washing machine, electric car charger and hot water around midday. A solar diverter can heat your water automatically from surplus power.
Keep off the grid at teatime. Between about 4pm and 7pm, let a battery or a delay timer cover what it can. This is when power is dearest, and the grid is under the most strain.
Buy the rest when it is cheap. In winter, solar may not cover all your needs. Use night or “boost” rates in the small hours to heat water, charge the car and top up the battery.

Then automate. Spain has offered households hourly prices since 2014, yet only 40% of those customers checked the cheapest hours before running big appliances. Timers and smart controls do it every day.

A colleague in our research group took this one step further. Rory Monaghan, a professor in energy systems engineering, wanted to know which electricity supplier and which plan really suited the way his household uses power. So he put his consumption and the available plans into a spreadsheet and ran an optimisation. The results were very different from what you would expect from the suppliers’ adverts. Electricity deals are confusing even for sustainability researchers.

Energy labels across Europe are being redesigned under the revised Energy Performance of Buildings Directive. This is the moment to rate buildings on how they behave, not just how they were designed: what they use, when they use it, and how they work with the grid.

Pakistan shows what happens when nobody is counting. Millions of buildings can remake an energy system faster than regulators can see it. Better to measure that change, and help every home run itself well, than to discover it from falling grid sales and have to rewrite the rules in a hurry.
