articles.title: Five ways that sea-level rise affects your daily life, even if you live inland
articles.author: Helen Millman, Postdoctoral Researcher, Polar Science, University of Exeter
paras: Rising sea levels might seem like someone else’s problem if you live inland. But, even miles from the coast, changing sea levels can affect the food we eat, the goods we buy, the energy we use and the taxes we pay.

Global sea levels are predicted to rise by between 28 and 55cm by 2100 if greenhouse gas emissions are significantly reduced. Sea levels could rise by between 63cm and 1m if emissions stay at very high levels. A rise of more than 2m by 2100 cannot be completely ruled out. Here’s how sea-level rise is already affecting our daily lives and exposing weaknesses in everything from power supplies to infrastructure:

The Fens, which spread across Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire and Norfolk, hold 48% of England’s best agricultural land and contribute over 7% of UK agricultural output, including about a third of England’s vegetables. Much of this landscape lies at or below sea level, which leaves it vulnerable to flooding and to contamination with saline water.

The land’s productivity depends on an extensive network of drainage channels, pumping stations and flood defences. A breach can destroy crops and leave productive soil unusable for years. As homegrown produce supplies only about 60% of the food the UK eats, losing Fens land alone would not empty shelves, although it would deepen reliance on imports that are themselves exposed to sea-level rise and other effects of climate change.
2. Disruption to port transport

Around 85% of the UK’s international freight by weight and more than 80% of world merchandise trade moves by sea. A flooded terminal at Southampton, in Shanghai or on a Caribbean island delays goods bound for shops and factories far inland.

Even if a port isn’t directly affected by floods, there can be disruption if the infrastructure connecting it to the rest of the economy is inundated. Railways, roads, warehouses, electrical substations and fuel distribution networks can all be affected by coastal flooding. The resulting shortages and price rises would have serious knock-on effects for households.
3. Damage to power supplies

The UK has three times more coastal energy facilities than any other European country. These facilities include oil refineries, fossil fuel and liquefied natural gas terminals, and nuclear power stations. Floodwater can inundate electrical equipment, damage control systems, disrupt fuel deliveries and cut off the roads and railways on which workers and suppliers depend, while saltwater can corrode infrastructure and complicate repairs.

Simultaneous damage to several facilities, or a prolonged interruption to a major fuel terminal or electricity connection, could make it harder to maintain reliable supplies. Even where electricity generation continues, damage to substations and other network infrastructure can prevent power from reaching consumers. This has implications for household energy bills, industrial production and the reliability of electricity supplies.
4. Risk to national security

The UK’s defence infrastructure is also threatened by sea-level rise. Naval bases, dockyards and other coastal facilities are exposed to rising sea levels and storm surges, potentially affecting access, operations and the infrastructure needed to maintain military capability. Keeping these sites functioning in coming decades will require action that may include relocating some of them.

Sea-level rise could also make the rest of the world a more dangerous place. Population displacement driven by climate pressures, including sea-level rise, places additional demands on humanitarian assistance and international cooperation. It also compounds any existing political and security pressures nationally.

The costs of sea-level rise fall on people across the country. Protecting vulnerable communities, subsidising flood insurance and relocating communities and infrastructure from areas that can no longer be defended will require substantial investment.

Meanwhile, the loss of productive farmland could push up food prices, and disruption to ports and transport links could make imported goods more expensive or harder to obtain. Damage to energy infrastructure could add further costs for households and businesses. The cumulative effect would be felt across the country through higher prices, higher taxes and reduced spending on other public services.

Rapid emissions reductions to keep overshoot of 1.5°C as brief and as low as possible are the safest way to reduce the rate and extent of sea level rise, and the associated costs of adapting. However, current global policies are projected to take us to about 2.8°C of warming. The UN’s upcoming climate summit, Cop31 in Turkey this November, will be a chance to close the gap between what has been promised and what is needed.

The world has already warmed by 1.4°C, so continued sea level rise is now inevitable even with rapid emissions reductions. Adaptation is as essential as mitigation. The design of sea defences and infrastructure need to be adapted accordingly as seas rise. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving coastal adaptation will help determine how severely sea level rise affects people, both inland and close to the coast.
Helen Millman sits on the advisory council of the Conservative Environment Network.

articles.title: Not in a FEMA flood zone? Your home could still be at risk – and you could suffer more than your neighbor
articles.author: Yilei Yu, Senior Researcher and Postdoctoral Fellow in Geography, Rice University
paras: If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.

Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more, and 14.6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated, and some are two decades old. Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.
But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.
FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.
To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed, including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.
Same street, different risks
When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.
The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding, even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.

One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.

Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.

We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.

Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.
The new research helps communities locate those homes.
4 things that make a home vulnerable
To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined four types of information about each home.

Water: How deep would floodwaters likely get at the home in a 100-year flood event, defined as having a 1% chance of occurrence in any given year? Here, we took a national flood model’s map of estimated parcel-level flood depths across Harris County and recorded the estimated depth at each residence.

Building: How old is the home, and how well has it been constructed and maintained? Older, lower-quality homes in poor repair tend to suffer more damage when floodwater enters the structure. County appraisal records collected by expert assessors can provide critical pieces of information for making such judgments.

Mobility: How busy are the roads nearby? For each home, we measured typical traffic within about a half-mile and within 3 miles. The busier those surrounding roads, the more a flood disrupts trips to work, school and hospitals, and the harder it is for first responders to get in and trapped residents to get out.
Finances: How much would it cost to repair the home, and what share of nearby homes have flood insurance? Neither keeps water out of a home, but both reflect what it costs to recover.

We chose these four criteria because flood research consistently highlights their importance for how hard a flood hits a community: how much water arrives, how well the building holds up, whether people can still get around and how big the repair bill is for the owner. They aren’t the only possible measures; a city could use others within each category, depending on available data.

Homes in the same neighborhood can have very different flood vulnerability scores. In fact, we found the scores differed more from house to house within a neighborhood than from one neighborhood to the next.

In practice, this means that knowing a neighborhood’s flood risk doesn’t necessarily tell you how hard a flood could hit any individual home. A neighborhood could look safe on average while containing some of the county’s riskiest homes, and there may be many well-protected homes in an otherwise risky neighborhood. Much of the problem, we show, lies at the scale of buildings, not neighborhoods or ZIP codes.
What residents and communities can do
Homeowners can check several of these risks themselves.

Ask longtime neighbors or your city’s flood plain office whether your home or the street has been flooded before. Look up the home’s age in local property records and have an inspector assess its condition. Find out whether the routes to work and school flood easily. And check whether you have a flood insurance policy, and what it covers: Most homeowner’s policies don’t cover flood damage.

Communities can apply our approach with their own data to locate particularly vulnerable housing where neighborhood averages may disguise the need for help. They can start with existing address-level flood scores, such as First Street’s, and add local records on buildings, roads and insurance. The extra details matter because officials have limited money for flood-proofing homes, improving drainage and helping families recover after floods. Better data on buildings and flood risk can help them invest wisely.
Data similar to that used for Houston exists across much of the United States, so other flood-prone cities could follow the same approach.
Floods don’t stop at the lines on a map, and they don’t hit every house on a street the same. We believe it’s time for residents and local flood authorities to prepare accordingly.
